The engine is otherwise unchanged and still carburetted.
Stock gearing on the 2011-2015 450 SX-F is 14/52 (3.71). Testers found it tall and ran 14/53; faster riders went to 13/50 (3.85) and one factory rider used 13/51.

The 2011-2012 450 SX-F has a 63.5 degree steering head angle. It tracks accurately, is stable at speed and less twitchy than the PDS bikes, but will not turn as tightly as the sharpest-steering Japanese 450 of the time.

On a magazine dyno the 2014 YZ450F made 58.17 hp at 9,900 rpm, 2.25 hp more than the 2013 at peak and 3 hp more at 7,500 rpm; at 11,000 rpm it was still above the 2013's peak. The runs used the magazine's own richer map; on the stock map the engine was lean, stuttered off idle and coughed on landings.

A magazine test crew's 2014 YZ450F setup: fork stock 4.9 N/mm springs, 335 cc oil (pros add 10 cc), compression 11 clicks out (stock 9), rebound 8 out, legs 4 mm up. Shock stock 58 N/mm spring, 105 mm sag (stock 100), high-speed compression 2 turns out (stock 1-1/2), low-speed 12 clicks out, rebound 9 out (stock 14). Rear sprocket 50 in place of 49.

statement: The 2014 YZ450F's stock map is lean. With the GYTR Power Tuner, testers ran richer fuel and more ignition advance; with the stock pipe a slightly richer fuel map on stock timing also works, and aftermarket pipes want a little more fuel than stock. Yamaha's 2015 stock map is close to that corrected map, so a 2014 can be remapped to match.

2015 YZ450F changes: stiffer fork springs (5.0 N/mm) with new valving and 10 cc less oil, a remapped ECU, a throttle return spring 20% lighter, steel lower engine mounts in place of aluminium, a 48-tooth rear sprocket (was 49), a roller gear-stop lever, quarter-turn fasteners on the airbox cover, black rims and Dunlop MX52 tyres.

A magazine test crew's 2015-2017 YZ450F setup: fork stock 5.0 N/mm springs, 315 cc oil, compression 10 clicks out (stock 8), rebound 8 out (stock 10), legs 4 mm up. statement: Launch control on the 2016-2017 YZ450F cuts power from 4,500 rpm at 30% throttle and gives it back after 30-60 ft or at the shift to third. The stock map gave the best all-round power in testing. With the Power Tuner, more ignition advance and slightly richer fuel up high sharpens it; for a mellower bike richen every fuel cell and retard every ignition cell at least 2 degrees. A flywheel weight also calms the corner-exit wheelie.

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2014-2017 YZ450F: vague, loose turn-in and a tall rear (raise the fork 4 mm, run 103-105 mm sag, fit a 143.5 mm aftermarket shock link, which drops the rear about 8 mm, and swap the stock front tyre for one suited to the dirt), a wide gap in the gearbox on the second-to-third shift (one tooth more on the rear), the quarter-turn airbox fasteners falling out or snagging on 2015-2016 bikes (tape them or go back to bolts), a grip that wears the rider's thumb raw (a grip donut), loud intake noise from the front airbox, brakes behind the class best and an exhaust that is very hard to remove (a long extension and a swivel 10 mm socket).

statement: The 2014-2017 YZ450F is stable and has the best stock suspension of its era, but the front feels heavy and wide and hunts on turn entry while the rear sits tall. The 2016 change to 25 mm offset and a softer shock spring helped without curing it. Reliability and the cable clutch were consistently praised.
